did_you_know.text: Hosea commands the trumpet to be blown and the alarm sounded because danger is approaching, described as coming swiftly and powerfully “like an eagle against the house of the LORD.” The reason for the danger is explicit: Israel has violated the covenant and rebelled against the law.

Although Israel cries out to the LORD and says that it knows Him, the chapter makes clear that their cries are not accompanied by actual faithfulness: they have rejected what is good, and therefore the enemy will pursue them.

The prophet criticizes Israel’s leadership because the kings and officials were appointed without the LORD’s approval. The same verse also describes their spending silver and gold to make idols, sealing their fate to be destroyed.
The calf of Samaria is presented as something rejected by the LORD: His anger burns against Israel, and the prophet asks how long they will remain unable to purify themselves from this act.

The prophet emphasizes that the calf of Samaria is not a deity from heaven but the work of a craftsman: “A craftsman made it; it is not God.” Therefore, it will become mere splinters—it will be broken and crumble.

The expression “They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind” presents a principle of retribution: unstable and worthless actions can bring a far more severe result. The grain mentioned in the verse also produces no flour, and even if it grows, foreigners will swallow it.

Israel is described as having been swallowed up among the nations and becoming a vessel that no one wants. The image expresses a loss of independence and value in the eyes of the nations, not merely material deprivation.

The chapter explicitly mentions turning to Assyria and Ephraim’s attempts to establish political relationships through gifts or payments, described by the words “they hired lovers.” According to the prophet, this policy will not save Israel but will instead bring about its dispersion.

The LORD says that even if He wrote out for Ephraim the many teachings of His law, they would regard them as something foreign. This emphasizes that the problem is not a lack of instruction, but the rejection of the existing law and treating it as though it did not belong to the people.

At the end of the chapter, forgetting the LORD is contrasted with extensive building: Israel built palaces, and Judah fortified cities, but human works will not protect them. The prophet declares that fire will consume the cities of Judah and its palaces.
